{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-tn","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"ee06cc2f35673a7909ff0c15f244c455c262c5b9bcf521200041daaad0e3e687","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-tn-class-d:lineage:28","source_registry_sha256":"8b0b6a068a0aa720d419171b5007a2610ed6c5012eeff522b57713cf9226eb71","source_liveness_sha256":"d27b9a94f03ec29d960b8eea38966606a7d3fdb703ad30b19ecd93f9bc70d0c7"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Traffic signs, signals and pavement markings","heading":"C — Traffic control devices: sign colors and shapes, stop, yield and railroad signs, regulatory signs, traffic lights and arrows, broken signals, pedestrian signals and pavement markings","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Traffic control devices: sign colors and shapes, stop, yield and railroad signs, regulatory signs, traffic lights and arrows, broken signals, pedestrian signals and pavement markings
Knowledge domain: how Tennessee drivers read traffic control devices — what each sign color and shape announces, what stop, yield and railroad signs require, how regulatory and warning signs work, what each signal light and arrow allows, what to do when a signal is dark, and what each pavement line and marking permits. Taught from the manual's text only; the pictured signs themselves are not described.

FACT_ID: sec07-F01 | anchor: A01
Directions from police, highway construction workers or school crossing guards must be obeyed even when they differ from what the signals and signs show. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0049]

FACT_ID: sec07-F02 | anchor: A01
Every sign's shape and color announce its purpose, so a stop sign hidden by dirt, branches or snow is still known by its red octagon. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0049]

FACT_ID: sec07-F03 | anchor: A01
A rectangular sign carries laws, regulations or instructions such as speed limits or lane use. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0049]

FACT_ID: sec07-F04 | anchor: A01
Red is the background only for stop signs, the four-way or all-way plates beneath them, do not enter and wrong way signs, and interstate route markers. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0049]

FACT_ID: sec07-F05 | anchor: A01
Orange backgrounds are reserved for construction and maintenance signs and are used for nothing else. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0049]

FACT_ID: sec07-F06 | anchor: A01
Yellow is the background for general warning signs, brown marks recreational and cultural points of interest, green is for guide signs and mileposts, and blue is for motorist services. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0049]

FACT_ID: sec07-F07 | anchor: A01
Fluorescent yellow-green is the color for school zone signs. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0049]

FACT_ID: sec07-F08 | anchor: A02
Fluorescent yellow-green signs also mark pedestrian areas such as crosswalks and are easier to see in low light, fog and rain. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0050]

FACT_ID: sec07-F09 | anchor: A02
Fluorescent pink, sometimes called coral, marks temporary traffic control for incidents such as crashes, wildfires, floods and hazardous material spills. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0050]

FACT_ID: sec07-F10 | anchor: A02
The octagon is the only eight-sided sign, always red with white letters, and requires a complete stop without passing the crosswalk. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0050]

FACT_ID: sec07-F11 | anchor: A02
If you cannot see cross traffic after stopping at a stop sign, creep forward carefully to where you can see and go only when it is safe. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0050]

FACT_ID: sec07-F12 | anchor: A02
A red ALL WAY plate under a stop sign means every direction of traffic at that intersection must stop. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0050]

FACT_ID: sec07-F13 | anchor: A02
At a triangular yield sign, slow down and stop for cross traffic coming from either side; with no cars coming you may enter carefully without a full stop, but always stop in heavy traffic. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0050]

FACT_ID: sec07-F14 | anchor: A02
The round railroad advance sign warns that a grade crossing is ahead, so slow down and be ready to stop if a train is coming. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0050]

FACT_ID: sec07-F15 | anchor: A02
Never try to beat a train, because drivers usually misjudge its speed, and the manual counts more than 200 crashes a year at railroad crossings. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0050]

FACT_ID: sec07-F16 | anchor: A02
The X-shaped crossbuck stands at every railroad grade crossing and marks exactly where the tracks are, with a small sign below showing how many tracks there are. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0050]

FACT_ID: sec07-F17 | anchor: A02
Flashing lights on a crossbuck mean a train is coming: stop, stay stopped until it passes, and make sure every track is clear before crossing. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0050]

FACT_ID: sec07-F18 | anchor: A02
Where a crossing has gates, stop when the lights start flashing and before the gate comes down, and wait until the gates rise and the lights stop. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0050]

FACT_ID: sec07-F19 | anchor: A02
Diamond-shaped signs warn of hazards or unexpected conditions ahead and usually call for slowing down. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0050]

FACT_ID: sec07-F20 | anchor: A03
Speed signs show the maximum allowed, the minimum required or a coming change in the limit. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec07-F21 | anchor: A03
A school speed sign run by a time clock flashes yellow lights while lighting up the limit, and it is posted wherever children may be walking across the street to or from school. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec07-F22 | anchor: A03
On a road with more than one lane each way, the keep-right sign means stay in the far right lane unless passing a slower car or turning left. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec07-F23 | anchor: A03
No-passing zones are set by how far ahead you can see, allowing for hidden hazards such as hills, curves, intersections and driveways. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec07-F24 | anchor: A03
The triangular No Passing Zone sign, yellow or orange, is placed on the left side of the road. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec07-F25 | anchor: A03
A red circle with a diagonal line on a white sign means the action pictured behind it is forbidden. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec07-F26 | anchor: A03
Standing in the roadway to ask for a ride is illegal in Tennessee. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec07-F27 | anchor: A07
Traffic lights run red, yellow and green from top to bottom, and the red light always means stop. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec07-F28 | anchor: A07
On a steady red, stop behind the crosswalk or stop line; unless a sign forbids it, you may then turn right once no pedestrians or cross traffic are present. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec07-F29 | anchor: A07
A yellow light means red comes next: slow to a smooth stop if you safely can, never speed up to beat it, and if you are already in the intersection keep going carefully. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec07-F30 | anchor: A07
Tennessee law requires the yellow light to show for at least three seconds before the red. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec07-F31 | anchor: A07
A green light lets you go only if the intersection is clear: yield to pedestrians and vehicles still in it, and to oncoming traffic when turning left. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec07-F32 | anchor: A07
With a green turn arrow you have the right-of-way to turn only that way, after yielding to anyone already in the intersection. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec07-F33 | anchor: A07
A yellow turn arrow means get ready to yield to oncoming traffic, and a red arrow or red light in your lane bans all turns even when other lanes have green. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec07-F34 | anchor: A07
A flashing yellow arrow lets you turn left only after yielding to all oncoming traffic and to bicyclists and pedestrians in the crosswalk. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec07-F35 | anchor: A07
A flashing red light is the same as a stop sign, and a flashing yellow light means slow down and go through carefully. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec07-F36 | anchor: A07
When a traffic signal is not working, Tennessee law treats the intersection as an all-way stop. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec07-F37 | anchor: A08
When two or more vehicles stop at an all-way stop at the same moment, the driver on the left yields to the driver on the right. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec07-F38 | anchor: A08
Tennessee law defines a pedestrian as anyone on foot or using a motorized or non-motorized wheelchair. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec07-F39 | anchor: A08
A solid white line marks the right edge of your lane, and a yellow line marks the left edge of lanes going your direction, so yellow on your right and white on your left means you are going the wrong way. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec07-F40 | anchor: A08
Yellow lines separate traffic moving in opposite directions. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec07-F41 | anchor: A08
A broken yellow center line may be crossed to pass when no traffic is coming and it is safe. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec07-F42 | anchor: A08
Double solid yellow lines may not be crossed to pass from either direction, though you may cross a solid yellow line to turn into a driveway or side road when safe. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec07-F43 | anchor: A09
With one solid and one broken yellow line, you may pass only when the broken line is on your side, and you must be back in your lane before the passing zone ends. [A09]
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec07-F44 | anchor: A09
White lines separate lanes going the same way: a broken white line may be crossed when safe, a solid white line means stay in your lane, and a double solid white line must not be crossed. [A09]
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec07-F45 | anchor: A09
Yield to pedestrians who are in a crosswalk or about to enter it, and remember that not every crosswalk is marked. [A09]
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec07-F46 | anchor: A09
Stop behind a painted stop line; with no stop line, stop before the first crosswalk line, and with neither, stop before your front bumper crosses the cross street's edge line. [A09]
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec07-F47 | anchor: A09
A lane marked with a curved arrow and the word ONLY must turn that way, while a lane showing both curved and straight arrows may turn or go straight. [A09]
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0057]

Misconceptions: a yellow light is not a signal to speed up; a green light does not erase the duty to yield; a dark signal is an all-way stop, not a free pass; a solid yellow line still lets you turn into a driveway; a red arrow bans the turn even when the next lane has green.
Mnemonics: eight sides, stop; three sides, yield; round means railroad ahead; X marks the tracks; yellow to your right means turn around.
Glossary: crossbuck means the X-shaped sign at a railroad crossing; protected arrow means a green turn arrow that gives you the right-of-way; permissive arrow means a flashing yellow arrow that allows a turn after yielding; stop line means the white line showing where to stop.
Dynamic facts: sign designs change as Tennessee updates to the federal uniform standards, so old and new signs can appear side by side; confirm current designs on official sources.
